Good afternoon, Chair Singh and members of Planning and Strategic Initiatives Committee.
Planning staff are proud to present to Council the Missing Middle and Affordable Housing Community Improvement Plan.
City of Kitchener has developed a missing middle in affordable housing community improvement
plan to help create more housing that people with different incomes can afford.
On March 2025, the city received an additional $4.2 million from the Housing Accelerator
Fund based on the success of our other half initiatives to establish a CIP.
The CIP builds on those efforts to increase the housing supply, building inclusive and
diverse communities by creating 98 units by October 2026 and 500 units over the next 10 years.
Of the 98 unit total, 49 units must be affordable and the remainder be within 1500 metres of rapid transit.
I'll highlight a few items about the program criteria.
This CIP applies to land situated within the City of Kitchener's municipal boundary.
Priority will be given to projects that achieve funding goals associated with the funding program
from other orders of government. Projects that are located within 1500 meters of rapid transit
that incorporate affordable housing units and that have a plan to achieve building permit issuance
by October 31st, 2026. Planning staff evaluated a few initiatives to determine which ones will have
the greatest long-term impact on housing affordability and availability. Staff have
focused on two initiatives. This first program is called the additional dwelling units grant.
Staff are proposing up to 100% development charge grants to help offset upfront costs
of developing ADUs.
Grants for the second and third dwelling unit shall cover 100% of the cost of applicable
educational development charges.
Grants for the fourth dwelling unit shall cover 50% of city, regional and educational
DCs as base incentive or 100% of city, regional and educational DCs for units that commit
to providing a minimum of one affordable housing unit for five years or energy efficiency measures
or one barrier-free unit.
Second program is called the Missing Middle Affordable Housing Grant.
This grant is offering up to $25,000 per affordable unit to a maximum of $500,000 per project.
This would help offset the costs associated with pre-construction planning, design and
approvals costs for affordable housing and missing middle built forms.
The types of costs that would qualify include but aren't limited to municipal and agency
fees and charges and consultant service fees, for example, planning, design, legal, property
appraisal, environmental and engineering.
Awarded projects must maintain affordable units for a minimum of 25 years from the date
of first occupancy and applicants should provide affordable units to priority groups as identified
through the City's Housing Needs Assessment.
We will be launching the CIP program in January.
We will return to Council with a progress report.
In closing, developed using an evidence-based approach, this policy integrates input from
